composition: The alloy is a low-density Fe-28Mn-8Al-1C steel (nominal composition in wt%), with measured contents of C 0.97, Mn 27.91, Al 8.04, S 0.004, P 0.006 wt% and Fe balance (Table 1). Iron is the matrix element; Mn acts as an austenite stabilizer, Al provides the low-density character (measured density 6.82 g cm⁻³), and C contributes to solid-solution strengthening. The high combined Mn, Al, and C additions produce a high-stacking-fault-energy (SFE), single-phase austenitic matrix, whose low yield strength motivates the cryogenic-rolling strengthening study.
conclusions: At 50% cryogenic rolling reduction, deformation twinning becomes the main plastic deformation mechanism while dislocation plane slip diminishes, marking the transition stage between the low-strain slip-dominated regime and the high-strain dislocation-cell/nanocrystalline regime. The sample exhibits a clear strength-ductility trade-off relative to the undeformed condition, with UTS rising from 882 to 1518 MPa, YS from 505 to 1379 MPa, and microhardness from 284 to 479 HV, while elongation falls from 64.5% (undeformed) to 8.8%. These intermediate-state results demonstrate how cryogenic rolling can be used to tune the microstructure and mechanical properties of low-density austenitic steel.
mechanisms: At 50% CR reduction, dislocation plane slip is suppressed and deformation twinning is activated: extensive dislocation multiplication within the slip planes hardens them, and back stress from dislocation pile-ups further impedes dislocation motion; as stress rises with continued deformation, cross-slip and deformation twinning are triggered, producing dislocation walls/entanglements alongside a significant amount of deformation twins.

The cryogenic environment enables twinning despite the high-SFE austenite: Al and C additions raise the room-temperature SFE (72 mJ m⁻²), but cooling to cryogenic temperature lowers it to 51 mJ m⁻²; combined with the restriction of dislocation motion at low temperature and localized stress concentration from accumulated dislocations, this promotes deformation twinning at moderate strain even though the SFE remains above the ≈20–40 mJ m⁻² range typical of twinning-induced plasticity steels.

The deformation substructure strengthens the material: the increased dislocation density creates dislocation forests that entangle and hinder dislocation motion (Taylor strain hardening), while grain refinement introduces boundaries that impede slip (Hall-Petch strengthening), raising the yield strength to 1379 MPa and UTS to 1518 MPa.

The strength gain is accompanied by a loss of ductility: a high initial dislocation density and refined structure limit further dislocation accumulation and strain-hardening capacity during tensile deformation, reducing elongation to 8.8% and refining/shallowing the ductile dimples on the fracture surface.
microstructure: The CR 50% sample retains a single-phase austenite (FCC) structure with no deformation-induced martensitic transformation, consistent with the OM, TEM, and XRD observations across the CR series. Optical microscopy reveals flattened/banded elongated grains along the rolling direction (RD) with dense slip bands. TEM shows that the distinct characteristics of dislocation plane slip have vanished at this reduction; instead, dislocation entanglements and dislocation walls emerge from dislocation-dislocation interactions, alongside a significant amount of fine parallel deformation twins. XRD line-profile analysis gives an austenite (220) peak FWHM of 0.776°, a microstrain of 5.1 × 10⁻³, and a calculated dislocation density of 7.9 × 10¹⁴ m⁻².
processing: The test steel was produced by vacuum melting and casting, then the ingot was heated to 1200 °C, held for 2 h, and hot forged into billets of 100 × 100 mm cross-section. Plate-shaped specimens were excised from the billet center along the forging direction. Prior to CR, all specimens were solution-treated at 1000 °C for 1 h and water-quenched to room temperature. For cryogenic rolling on an LG-300 two-high rolling mill, the specimens were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 3–5 min; after cooling, each specimen was rapidly removed for a single rolling pass with a thickness reduction of about 2%, then promptly re-immersed in liquid nitrogen. This immersion/rolling cycle was repeated until the cumulative thickness reduction reached 50%.
properties: Tensile testing of dog-bone-shaped specimens (20 × 5 × 1 mm standard gauge segment) machined along RD, conducted at a strain rate of 0.2 mm min⁻¹, gives a yield strength of 1379 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 1518 MPa, and an elongation of 8.8%. Microhardness, measured with a 500 g load and 15 s dwell time and averaged over at least five measurements, is 479 HV. The alloy density is 6.82 g cm⁻³. After tensile failure, SEM fractography shows uniformly distributed dimples of reduced size and depth relative to the undeformed and CR 30% conditions, indicating retained ductile fracture with reduced ductility. The sample was characterized by OM (etched with hydrochloric acid + alcohol + copper chloride), SEM (fractography), TEM (dislocation substructure and twins), and XRD (phase identification, peak broadening, microstrain, and dislocation density).
summary: This specimen is a low-density Fe-28Mn-8Al-1C austenitic steel that was solution-treated at 1000 °C for 1 h, water-quenched, and then cryogenically rolled (CR) to a cumulative thickness reduction of 50%. It is one of four CR states (30%, 50%, 70%, 90%) used to systematically investigate how cryogenic rolling governs the interplay between dislocation slip and deformation twinning and the resulting strength-ductility trade-off.
unmapped: The SFE of this steel is 72 mJ m⁻² at room temperature and 51 mJ m⁻² at cryogenic temperature.
